lead: A tension test pulls a specimen until it breaks and records load against extension. Dividing load by the original area gives stress; dividing extension by the original gauge length gives strain. The plot of one against the other is the stress-strain diagram, the material's signature. Its shape separates ductile materials, which stretch a lot before breaking, from brittle materials, which do not. Designers read yield strength, ultimate strength, stiffness and ductility from this one curve. It sets safe working stresses for beams, shafts and bolts.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for the definitions of normal stress σ = P/A and normal strain ε = ΔL/L.

sections.h3: The test and the two axes

blocks.text: A tension test pulls a standard specimen until it breaks. The specimen is a round bar of known diameter d, or a flat strip of known width and thickness. A marked length in the middle is the gauge length L₀. The machine records the load P and the extension ΔL at each instant.

items: Measure the original diameter d and mark the gauge length L₀.
Mount the specimen in the testing machine and apply load slowly.
Record load P against extension ΔL until the specimen breaks.
Convert the record to stress and strain and plot the curve.

blocks.text: Engineering stress divides the load by the original area. Engineering strain divides the extension by the original gauge length. Both use original dimensions, so any laboratory gets the same curve for the same material.

blocks.where: σ is the engineering stress in N/mm², which is the same as MPa; P is the tensile load in N; A₀ is the original cross-section area in mm².
ε is the engineering strain, a pure number; ΔL is the change in gauge length in mm; L₀ is the original gauge length in mm. Percentage strain is 100ε.

blocks.text: The plot of σ against ε is the material's signature. The first straight part means stress is proportional to strain; its slope is Young's modulus E, taken up in Chapter 1.4. The test assumes the material is homogeneous (the same everywhere) and isotropic (the same in every direction).
Mild steel is the reference ductile material. Its curve has five named parts.

items: Proportional limit: the straight part from the origin. Up to this point σ/ε is constant.
Elastic limit: the highest stress the specimen can take and still return to its original length. For metals it sits just above the proportional limit.

Yield: the curve drops suddenly. The peak is the upper yield point; the dip that follows is the lower yield point; the flat stretch after the dip is the yield plateau. Along the plateau, strain grows with almost no extra load. Designers take the lower yield stress as the yield strength.
Strain hardening: after the plateau, stress rises again as the crystal structure tangles. The peak is the ultimate tensile strength (UTS).
Necking and fracture: past the peak the bar thins into a neck, the load falls, and the specimen breaks.

blocks.text: The stress at fracture, still computed with A₀, is the breaking stress. For mild steel it is lower than the UTS because the neck carries the load on a smaller area. The metal itself has not softened. In the figure, the vertical drop to zero at the end marks fracture; the breaking stress is the last non-zero stress before that drop.
The figure uses values close to a real test: yield near 229 MPa at about 0.11% strain, so the initial slope is about 200 GPa; UTS near 446 MPa; fracture after about 24% strain.

sections.h3: Brittle material and the offset proof stress

blocks.text: Cast iron, concrete, glass and many ceramics are brittle. Their curve is almost straight and then stops. There is no yield plateau, so fracture and maximum stress are almost the same point. Failure comes without visible warning.

Without a yield point, we use an offset proof stress. Draw a line parallel to the initial straight part, starting at 0.2% strain on the horizontal axis. Where it cuts the curve is the 0.2% proof stress. It is the stress that leaves a permanent strain of 0.2% after unloading. Some alloys use 0.1% instead.

items: Yield strength: the stress at first permanent set; for brittle materials, the proof stress.
Ultimate tensile strength (UTS): the highest stress on the engineering curve.
Breaking strength: the stress at fracture, using A₀.
Percentage elongation: (L_f − L₀)/L₀ × 100, where L_f is the fractured gauge length. It measures ductility.

blocks.text: Ductile steels commonly show 20–30% elongation; brittle cast iron shows under 1%. Thin sections, sharp corners and low temperature make brittle fracture more likely.

figure.caption: Stress against strain from a tension test. The steel curve (MS) has a yield step, a long rising plastic region and a necking fall; the cast-iron curve (C) breaks almost at its peak, with no plastic stretch. The elastic part of MS is drawn to give the correct slope (about 200 GPa); the vertical drop at the end of each curve marks fracture, and the breaking stress is the last non-zero point.

spec.aria: The mild-steel curve has a yield region and long plastic stretch; the cast-iron curve breaks with little plastic strain.

examples.question: A mild steel specimen has gauge length 50 mm and diameter 10 mm. It yields at a load of 18 kN, reaches an ultimate load of 35 kN, and the fractured gauge length is 62 mm. Find the yield stress, the ultimate tensile strength and the percentage elongation.
steps: Original area: A₀ = πd²/4 = π(10 mm)²/4 = 78.54 mm².
Yield stress: σ_y = P_y/A₀ = 18 000 N / 78.54 mm² = 229.2 N/mm² = 229.2 MPa.
Ultimate stress: σ_u = P_u/A₀ = 35 000 N / 78.54 mm² = 445.6 MPa.
examples.answer: Yield stress is 229.2 MPa, ultimate tensile strength is 445.6 MPa, and percentage elongation is 24%.
examples.check:
import math
d = 10.0
L0 = 50.0
A0 = math.pi * d**2 / 4
print(round(A0, 2))
print(round(18000 / A0, 1))
print(round(35000 / A0, 1))
print(round((62 - L0) / L0 * 100, 1))

traps: Engineering stress uses the original area A₀. Dividing by the neck area gives true stress, which is a different quantity.
The ultimate load is the maximum load, not the breaking load. For mild steel the breaking load is lower than the ultimate load.
Brittle materials have no yield plateau. A question asking for the yield strength of cast iron expects the 0.2% proof stress.
The 0.2% offset starts at strain 0.002. On a percentage-strain axis, start at 0.2 on that axis; on a plain strain axis, start at 0.002. Check which axis the question uses.
Percentage elongation uses the change over the original gauge length. MPa and N/mm² are the same unit.

quiz.q: Define gauge length and engineering stress.
quiz.a: Gauge length L₀ is the marked original length over which extension is measured. Engineering stress is σ = P/A₀, where P is the load and A₀ is the original cross-section area.

quiz.q: Why does the slope of the initial straight part of the stress-strain curve equal Young's modulus?
quiz.a: In that straight part stress is proportional to strain, so σ = Eε. The slope of the σ against ε line is therefore E.

quiz.q: A 12 mm diameter specimen yields at a load of 25 kN. Find the yield stress.
Curve A has a long yield plateau and 25% elongation; curve B is almost straight to fracture at 1% strain. Identify each type and state one design precaution for B.
quiz.a: A is ductile and gives warning before failure; B is brittle and fails suddenly. For B, keep working stress well below the proof stress and avoid sharp corners that concentrate stress.
It is the stress found where a line parallel to the initial straight part, drawn from 0.2% strain, cuts the curve. It leaves a permanent strain of 0.2% on unloading.

quiz.q: A specimen of gauge length 80 mm breaks with a fractured gauge length of 88 mm. Find the percentage elongation.
Why is the breaking stress lower than the UTS for mild steel but nearly equal for cast iron?
quiz.a: Mild steel forms a neck after the UTS, so the load falls while the original area is still used in the calculation. Cast iron does not neck; it separates almost at the peak load.

quiz.q: Why do we use original dimensions in engineering stress and strain?
quiz.a: Original dimensions are fixed before the test, so the curve depends only on the material and not on the current size of the specimen.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real curves are recorded with extensometers and processed by software; true stress uses the instantaneous area and keeps rising past the ultimate point. Modern work adds digital image correlation, high-temperature testing, high-strain-rate testing and anisotropy of rolled sheets. Search 'true stress true strain', '0.2% offset yield', 'tensile test standard' and 'ductile-to-brittle transition'.
